thread.title: Technology Select Sector Index Looking Ready For A Starter Position - Direxion Technology Bull 3x Shares ETF (NYSEARCA:TECL)

author: Todd Akin
title: Technology Select Sector Index Looking Ready For A Starter Position - Direxion Technology Bull 3x Shares ETF (NYSEARCA:TECL)
text:
The Direxion Technology Bull 3x Shares ETF ( TECL ) has reached the levels necessary to warrant a starter a position in shares. The ETF is down over 80 points from its highs set earlier in 2018 and, while there still seems to be considerable downside left in this market, the upside is so great that it makes sense to start nibbling.
The hope is that TECL falls to the $70s and $80s, in which point I would get to double down on my position. Then, if TECL moves lower from the $70s to the $50s, that would be the 2016 breakout level, which represents an area of significant value. Conversely, if I don't initiate a position here, there is a chance that the bottom could come based solely on the fact that indexes have had over a 10% fall from their highs, which is considered healthy in a bull market.
There is the pervasive narrative that the bull market run is over for stocks, and a bear market looms. However, macro indicators for the U.S. economy are strong (strong GDP, high employment rate, interest rates still being relatively low, cheap gas prices, etc.).
So, let's take a look at the data below in order to confirm if starting a position in TECL is the right move or not for investor's portfolios who are employing similar strategies.
TECL Overview TECL is considered a riskier ETF since it is triple leveraged and uses derivatives and other financial instruments to accomplish their goals, which can lead to magnified losses.
But, if the direction the investor picks is correct for triple leveraged ETFs, the reward can be quite large. TECL has a 1.09% expense ratio, which is a little high, but small in the scheme of things if the play works out. Here is a more thorough description of TECL below.
The investment seeks daily investment results- before fees and expenses- of 300% of the daily performance of the Technology Select Sector Index. The fund invests at least 80% of its net assets (plus borrowing for investment purposes) in securities of the index- ETFs that track the index and other financial instruments that provide daily leveraged exposure to the index or ETFs that track the index. The index includes domestic companies from the technology sector. It is non-diversified.
TECL Holdings Not only does TECL mimic the Technology Select Sector, but 68.86% of its holdings are in the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLK ), seen below.
Source: Seeking Alpha
So, since the XLK represents are large percentage of TECL's holdings, one must look at the holdings of XLK to get a better view of what TECL is actually trading on.
According to the data below, Microsoft ( MSFT ), Apple Inc. ( AAPL ), Intel ( INTC ), Cisco Systems ( CSCO ), and Visa Inc Class A ( V ) constitute as the top five holdings of XLK, and their allocation amount in the fund is a testament to that.
Source: Seeking Alpha
If an investor said that this skewed allocation could be seen as overloading into too few names, they would be right. Apple, which represents 17.5% of XLK, has pulled back significantly and only trades at 13.5x earnings. However, it still has room to fall before reaching 2015 support levels, which would be equivalent to about $140-$150 per share.
Microsoft, the largest holding of TECL, has barely even budged during this market meltdown, and still trades at a higher multiple of around 24x earnings. So, if that holding in MSFT finally caves to the market pressure, TECL could see a precipitous fall.
More importantly, the future of TECL hinges on the success of these two giants, which has made me sell in frustration in past occasions when Apple, let's say, would drag the entire index down in sympathy with it, diversified ETF or not.
Now that we have laid out the thesis for owning TECL, what the fund is, and what holdings it owns, now it is time to determine if the time is right or not to start a position. After all, most investors are aware of the quality of TECL's holdings, the question is whether it is the right time to buy them or not.
As one can see below, a one year chart of TECL is showing a break of the $100 support area, which is bearish by all measures. Source: E*TRADE
However, one could argue that the ETF is down over $80 points from its highs now at this point, and is starting to show value. Where the next support level lies, therefore, is key because if it is close by, obviously the downside risk is limited, and it doesn't hurt the portfolio much if a position is started here.
Technicals On A Max Timeframe The max timeframe of TECL tells a much different story than the one-year chart. As investors can see below, $75 looks to be the next support level, which would be the 200 day moving average and 2017 breakout level. Source: E*TRADE
The RSI of TECL is also oversold, which is bullish. So, a dip to $75 would ensure an oversold condition, which usually prompts a rally in share prices for any stock or ETF. It is important to note, though, that TECL's leveraged nature exaggerates the RSI. Consequently, investors would be wise to refer to the parent index of TECL, which is the Technology Select Sector Index (IXT).
Technology Select Sector Index According to the chart below, the IXT is approaching 2000 resistance levels of around $600 per share, which would now act as support in the world of trading. Source: E*TRADE
So, not only does support lie just underneath current levels of around $650.00, but the RSI would get to come down to healthier levels in order to, perhaps, justify some institutional buying. Also, to finish my previous point alluded to above, TECL's RSI was indeed misleading because IXT's RSI is showing to be nowhere near oversold conditions.
Regardless, 50 on the RSI acted as solid support on numerous occasions since 2010, and this level is where IXT is virtually sitting on top of. So, this $600 area could be the bottom for IXT since it acted as support in the year 2000, which would be the equivalent of the $70s to $80s in TECL where my next round of buying would occur.
If $600 is broken, look for the $400 area to be the next area of support, which would be the $50 level for TECL. Yes, this is a lot of pain to take. But, if one takes a starter position to pyramid into TECL, let's say using a 2+4+8 strategy, then owning 2K to now and 4K around the subsequent $75 level, means you can only lose 2K if shares fall 50% to the $50 area from here as I write this article (around $90-$100 a share).
For my portfolio, that is not a big risk, especially when doubling down on shares at $50 provides me with over a 150% gain if the former highs were to be reached again. This could all be done, just to think, while taking minimal pain with a starter position from these levels. Seems like a valid proposition if you are a long term investor trying to pick away at the indexes at attractive values for retirement.
Conclusion TECL has some downside left in shares, but prices have fallen enough to warrant a starter position in this $90 range, especially since the U.S. economy remains strong. I would not suggest this vehicle as a trade at the moment since one-year support was just broken, and the market remains treacherous.
However, investors with a longer term horizon may want to consider picking away at TECL here and in the $70s, taking minimal pain in the more extreme scenario of a fall to $50, and then doubling down on shares at that level.
It is important to note that when the market resumes its uptrend one day, TECL should be one of the indexes to participate in the rally due to its highly cyclical/risk-on nature. Sometimes having over 150% upside in a stock, alone, is not enough to justify a large position since it may not participate in a market rally. But, owning TECL decreases the odds of FOMO (fear of missing out) in a strong market rally while diversifying risk across multiple stocks.
Nonetheless, I am starting a position in TECL at current levels, and will add to positions further if the opportunities arise.
Disclosure: I am/we are long TECL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
